title: Covalent bonding
learningObjective: Know that a covalent bond is formed between atoms by the sharing of a pair of electrons; Understand covalent bonds in terms of electrostatic attractions; Understand how to use dot-and-cross diagrams to represent covalent bonds in: diatomic molecules, including hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, halogens and hydrogen halides; inorganic molecules, including water, ammonia and carbon dioxide; organic molecules containing up to two carbon atoms, including methane, ethane, ethene and those containing halogen atoms; Explain why substances with a simple molecular structure are gases or liquids, or solids with low melting and boiling points; Understand that the term intermolecular forces of attraction can be used to represent all forces between molecules; Explain why the melting and boiling points of substances with simple molecular structures increase, in general, with increasing relative molecular mass; Explain why substances with giant covalent structures are solids with high melting and boiling points; Explain how the structures of diamond, graphite and C₆₀ fullerene influence their physical properties, including electrical conductivity and hardness; Know that covalent compounds do not usually conduct electricity

sections.title: Covalent bonding — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Chapter 7 (u1:c07) explained compounds built by electron **transfer** — metals
handing electrons to non-metals to make ions. This chapter explains the other,
even bigger family of compounds: the ones built by electron **sharing**. Water,
the sugar in your food, the carbon dioxide you breathe out, the plastics in your
pencil case — almost every substance around you that is not a metal, not a salt
and not a rock mineral is held together by covalent bonds. There are far more
covalent compounds than ionic compounds, and by the end of this lesson the bond
that holds them together will feel routine rather than mysterious.

All eight objectives of record for this lesson are **core** specification
statements — examined in **both Paper 1 (1C) and Paper 2 (2C)**, and shared
with Science Double Award:

- a covalent bond is a **shared pair of electrons** (spec 1.44);
- covalent bonds explained as **electrostatic attractions** (spec 1.45);
- **dot-and-cross diagrams** for diatomic molecules (hydrogen, oxygen,
  nitrogen, the halogens and hydrogen halides), inorganic molecules (water,
  ammonia, carbon dioxide) and organic molecules up to two carbons (methane,
  ethane, ethene and halogen-containing ones) (spec 1.46);
- why **simple molecular structures** are gases, liquids or low-melting solids,
  and the term **intermolecular forces of attraction** (spec 1.47);
- why melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances **increase as
  relative molecular mass increases** (spec 1.48);
- why **giant covalent structures** are solids with high melting and boiling
  points (spec 1.49);
- how the structures of **diamond, graphite and C₆₀ fullerene** decide their
  properties — conductivity and hardness (spec 1.50);
- covalent compounds **do not usually conduct electricity** (spec 1.51).

The lesson runs in four movements: what a covalent bond is and how you draw it
(dot-and-cross, molecule by molecule); the shapes molecules take and the
special cases that break the 8-electron pattern; why molecular substances melt
and boil so easily — the intermolecular-forces story; and the giant covalent
counter-examples, diamond and graphite, where the same shared-pair idea builds
the hardest natural material on Earth. Work through the sections in order —
each one's skill feeds the next.

:::prior-knowledge
Three pieces of earlier work carry this whole lesson. First,
**electronic configurations** from Chapter 3 (u1:c03) — you need [2, 8, 7] for
chlorine or [2, 6] for oxygen without hesitation, because covalent bonding is
outer-shell bookkeeping. Second, **groups of the Periodic Table** from Chapter
4 (u1:c04) — the group number tells you the number of outer-shell electrons,
which decides how many bonds an atom forms. Third, **ionic bonding** from
Chapter 7 (u1:c07) — every idea here is its mirror image: sharing instead of
transfer, molecules instead of lattices, low melting points instead of high.
If any of those feels shaky, revisit it before going further.
:::

:::exam-hint
Every objective in this lesson is core — Paper 1 or Paper 2, every candidate
including Double Award. The single most examined skill is **drawing
dot-and-cross diagrams** (spec 1.46): it appears in some form in nearly every
paper, and the diagram rules are mechanical once learned. The second most
examined idea is the **melting-point argument** (specs 1.47–1.49): "which
forces break, and how much energy does that take?" Learn the two stories —
weak intermolecular forces for molecular substances, strong covalent bonds for
giant structures — and you can answer a whole family of 4–6 mark questions
almost on autopilot.
:::

:::misconception
"Covalent bonding is a completely new topic — nothing from ionic bonding
carries over." The opposite: it is the **same electrostatic idea pointed at a
different arrangement**. In both bond types the thing holding atoms together
is positive–negative attraction; the difference is only what the electrons do
(transfer versus share). Learners who file the two bond types as unrelated
subjects memorise twice. Learners who see sharing as transfer's twin need to
learn half as much — and exam questions frequently ask you to compare the two
in a single answer.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44–1.51 items — the eight-objective map, the
both-papers route badge, and the contrast with Chapter 7's transfer model. If
you can state all eight objectives in your own words and explain in one
sentence why covalent compounds outnumber ionic compounds in everyday matter,
you are ready for the sections that follow.
:::

sections.title: The covalent bond — shared pairs of electrons
sections.markdown:
Every bond you will meet on this course — ionic, covalent, metallic — is held
together by the same physics: **electrostatic attractions between something
positively charged and something negatively charged**. What makes a
**[[covalent-bond]]** different is the arrangement. In a covalent bond, a
**pair of electrons is shared between two atoms**. The shared pair sits
between the two nuclei, and both nuclei (positive) pull on it (negative) at
the same time. That two-way pull — the [[electrostatic-attraction]] between
the shared pair and *both* nuclei — is what locks the atoms together.

It is worth drawing the picture in your head precisely: two positive nuclei,
and between them one negative pair that belongs to neither atom alone. Each
nucleus is attracted to the shared pair; the pair is attracted to each
nucleus; and those pulls hold the two atoms at a fixed distance apart. Pull
them apart and you remove that attraction — which costs energy. This is the
whole bonding model in one paragraph, and every diagram later in this lesson
is just this picture with real atoms dropped in.

In most of the simple examples you will meet at International GCSE, each atom
supplies **one electron** to the shared pair — one from atom A, one from atom
B. That does not have to be so: both electrons of the shared pair may come
from the same atom. You will meet a few examples of this sharing pattern later
in the course, but the one-each arrangement is the one to picture by default.

:::key-point
When atoms have 8 electrons in their outer shell, they have the same number of
electrons as a noble gas atom — they are **[[isoelectronic]]** with a noble
gas. This is the target state that covalent bonding reaches for: each atom in
a molecule counts the shared electrons as part of its own outer shell, so
bonding arrangements that give every atom 2 (for hydrogen) or 8 outer
electrons are the ones that form.
:::

:::exam-hint
Dots and crosses are pure bookkeeping. The electrons drawn as dots and the
electrons drawn as crosses are **absolutely identical in reality** — there is
no difference between them at all. The only job of dots-versus-crosses is to
show which atom each electron came from. In an exam answer, never write that
"dot electrons" and "cross electrons" behave differently; and never be alarmed
if your own diagram mixes them — the examiner reads the *pairs*, not the
symbols.
:::

:::misconception
"A shared pair of electrons belongs to whichever atom it is drawn closer to."
No — the pair is shared, meaning both atoms count it in their outer shells
simultaneously. A related error is treating the shared pair as a kind of glue
stuck on the outside of one atom. The correct picture is a pair sitting
between the two nuclei, attracting and attracted by both at once. If your
diagram or your sentence assigns the pair exclusively to one atom, you have
drawn an ion, not a covalent bond.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44 and 1.45 items — defining a covalent bond as a
shared pair of electrons and explaining the holding force as electrostatic
attraction between the nuclei and the shared pair. The bank's marking points
want both halves: the definition *and* the mechanism. Practise writing the
one-sentence version: "a covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons
attracted to the nucleus of both atoms."
:::

sections.title: Covalent bonding in a hydrogen molecule
sections.markdown:
The simplest covalent substance on the course is hydrogen gas, and it is the
best place to see the shared pair in action. Covalent bonds are shown using a
**[[dot-and-cross-diagram]]** — and for hydrogen, the diagram is almost
suspiciously simple. Each hydrogen atom has one electron. Two hydrogen atoms
each put their single electron into a shared pair, and that pair sits between
the two nuclei. Both nuclei pull on the pair; the pair holds on to both atoms.
Hydrogen atoms therefore form **[[molecule]]s with the formula H₂** — two atoms
joined by one covalent bond — and the bond between them is very strong.

When you draw the diagram yourself, show each atom's single electron — one as
a dot, one as a cross — overlapping in the middle so the shared pair is
unmistakable. Around each atom, the pair completes a two-electron shell: the
same electron count as a helium atom. That is the covalent version of reaching
a noble gas arrangement, and it is the reason H₂ forms at all.

Two atoms per molecule is common enough to have its own name: molecules that
contain two atoms are called **[[diatomic]]**. Hydrogen is diatomic, and so are
the oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine and hydrogen-chloride molecules you will draw
in the next few sections. Molecules in general contain a fixed number of atoms
joined by covalent bonds — two for diatomic gases, three for water, five for
methane, and at the extreme, thousands of atoms for giant biological molecules
such as proteins and DNA. The word "fixed" matters: a real molecule always
contains exactly its own count of atoms, which is what lets you write a
formula like H₂ or CH₄ at all.

:::key-point
A molecule is a **fixed** number of atoms joined by covalent bonds. H₂ is
always two atoms; H₂O is always three. That fixed count is why molecular
substances have clean chemical formulae, and it is also the feature that
separates molecules from the giant structures you meet at the end of this
lesson, where no such fixed count exists.
:::

:::exam-hint
If a question asks you to "draw a dot-and-cross diagram for hydrogen", draw
the two overlapping circles with **one dot and one cross in the overlap** and
label the nuclei. Do not draw extra shells — hydrogen has only one shell, and
padding it out with invented electrons loses the mark. For "outer shell
electrons only" questions, hydrogen's entire configuration *is* its outer
shell, so a single circle per atom is the complete answer.
:::

:::misconception
"When two hydrogen atoms bond, they merge into one helium atom." They do not —
sharing electrons changes nothing about the nuclei. Each atom in the molecule
still carries exactly one proton and is still hydrogen; only the *electron
arrangement* is shared. The test of what an atom is, is the number of protons
in its nucleus, and that never changes in covalent bonding. You will see this
misconception dismantled properly in the next section — keep it in mind every
time a diagram makes a bonded atom look like a noble gas.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44 and 1.46 items — the H₂ dot-and-cross diagram
and the definition of a diatomic molecule. The bank drills the diagram under
exam constraints (outer electrons only, both electron origins shown) and the
vocabulary ("diatomic", "molecule") as one-mark recall items.
:::

sections.title: Noble gas structures — the 2-or-8 rule for covalent bonding
sections.markdown:
Why does hydrogen stop at H₂ and never form H₃? The answer is the counting
rule that organises almost everything in this chapter. In H₂, each hydrogen
atom has only one electron to share, so it can form **only one covalent bond**.
Once that single shared pair is in place, each atom's outer shell holds two
electrons — the same count as a helium atom, so each atom is
[[isoelectronic]] with a noble gas. There is nothing left to share, so no
third atom can join: the molecule is complete.

For every element except hydrogen, the target count is **eight** outer-shell
electrons. In virtually all the molecules you will meet at this level,
electrons are shared so that each hydrogen atom ends up with 2 electrons in
its outer shell and every other atom ends up with 8. Some books of mnemonics
call this the "octet rule" — the rule of eight. The counting convention that
makes it work is crucial: **shared electrons count as belonging to the outer
shells of both atoms at once.** One shared pair delivers one new electron to
each atom's count. Draw the overlap, count each atom's electrons (its own plus
its share of every pair), and check the totals: 2 for hydrogen, 8 for the rest.

Does reaching a noble-gas electron count mean the atom *becomes* a noble gas?
It does not — and this check matters. Sharing electrons changes nothing in the
nucleus. The number of protons is untouched, and it is the proton count that
defines what an atom is. A hydrogen atom in H₂ is still hydrogen even though
it is isoelectronic with helium; a chlorine atom sharing a pair in HCl is
still chlorine even though its outer-shell count matches argon. Isoelectronic
is about electron *counts*, never about element *identity*.

The rule has a structure to it as well as a number. When one atom sits in the
middle with others attached to it — as in methane, ammonia or water — the
**outer** atoms virtually always end up with 8 outer electrons (or 2 if they
are hydrogen). It is genuinely hard to find an exception. The **central** atom
is a different story: a few molecules exist where it ends up with more or
fewer than 8, and you will meet the famous examples in section 14.

:::key-point
Stability is an energy statement. When chemists say something is "more
stable", they usually mean it has **less energy** — the lower the energy, the
more stable. Hold a book in the air and let go: it drops to the floor, a
lower-energy position, and stays there. Chemical changes happen for the same
reason. **When bonds form, energy is given out**, so the bonded substance has
less energy than the separate atoms and is more stable. That is why bonds
form at all — and why you must supply energy to break them again.
:::

:::exam-hint
The 2-or-8 count is the fastest self-check in the whole topic. After drawing
any dot-and-cross diagram, count every atom's outer shell (own electrons +
shared electrons). If an outer hydrogen is not on 2, or an outer non-hydrogen
is not on 8, the diagram is wrong — fix it before moving on. Examiners award
the mark for correct sharing, and this ten-second audit catches nearly every
slip: missed pairs, doubled pairs, electrons dropped while copying from your
own working.
:::

:::misconception
"An atom bonded covalently has turned into a noble gas — hydrogen in H₂ *is*
helium." Electron counts can match while the atoms stay utterly different.
Identity is set by protons, and sharing electrons moves no protons. The
correct phrasing for the exam is that the atoms are **isoelectronic with** a
noble gas — the same number of electrons — never that they become it. Watch
also for the mirror-image error: claiming a bonded atom "has a full outer
shell so it is unreactive like a noble gas". Reactivity belongs to the
molecule as a whole, not to a noble-gas costume worn by one atom.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44 and 1.45 items — applying the 2-or-8 counting
rule and explaining bond formation through energy released and stability
gained. The bank's explain questions ask "why do atoms share electrons?" —
the marking points are the noble-gas electron count, the energy drop on bond
formation, and the counting convention that shared electrons belong to both
atoms.
:::

sections.title: Why does hydrogen form molecules?
sections.markdown:
Section 4 gave you the counting rule; this section gives you the *reason* the
rule works, and it is worth a section of its own because the same reasoning
answers every "why do bonds form?" question on the course.

**Whenever a bond is formed — of whatever kind — energy is released**, and the
things involved end up more stable (lower in energy) than they were before.
The more bonds an atom can form, the more energy is released, and the more
stable the resulting system becomes. Two separate hydrogen atoms sit high in
energy. Let them share a pair, and the H₂ molecule that forms is **much more
stable** than the two atoms were apart. The molecule is the lower-energy
state, which is why hydrogen gas exists as H₂ molecules and why the atoms
stay bonded rather than drifting apart again.

This energy story is also the exact reverse of bond breaking. If forming a
bond releases energy, then breaking a bond must **take in** the same amount
of energy — you have to climb back up to the separated-atom state. Keep this
pair of statements together in your mind:

- bond **formation** → energy **released** → products more stable;
- bond **breaking** → energy **supplied** → separates into higher-energy pieces.

You will use both directions constantly. In this chapter they explain why
molecular substances melt and boil at low temperatures (breaking the weak
forces between molecules costs little energy) while giant structures like
diamond demand enormous temperatures (breaking strong covalent bonds costs a
lot). In the energetics chapter (u3:c19) the same ideas become exothermic and
endothermic reactions properly. Learn them once, in the bonding context,
where the picture is simplest.

:::exam-hint
"Explain why hydrogen exists as H₂ molecules" is a two-mark gift if you speak
the energy language: (1) forming the bond **releases energy**, so (2) the
molecule is **more stable** (lower energy) than the separate atoms. The
mark scheme wants the energy movement named explicitly — answers that only
say "because they share electrons" describe *what* happens without the *why*.
The phrase "more stable than the separate atoms" is worth memorising as a
unit.
:::

:::misconception
"Hydrogen atoms *want* to reach a full shell, so they bond." Atoms do not want
anything — this teleology language costs marks in explanation questions. The
mechanical reason is energy: the bonded arrangement has **less energy** than
the separated atoms, and lower-energy arrangements are the stable ones.
Everything else — full shells, noble-gas counts — is a pattern we observe in
*which* arrangements win, not a desire the atoms feel. In your written
answers, replace every "wants", "tries" and "needs to" with an energy
statement and the mark scheme will find your reasoning where it looks for it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44 and 1.45 items — bond formation as an energy-
releasing process and stability as lower energy. The bank pairs this with
bond-breaking questions (energy supplied) so both directions of the energy
argument become automatic before the melting-point sections put them to work.
:::

sections.title: Covalent bonding in a hydrogen chloride molecule
sections.markdown:
Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is the first [[dot-and-cross-diagram]] with two different
atoms, and it introduces three drawing conventions you will use for the rest
of the course.

The chemistry first. A chlorine atom has 7 electrons in its outer shell. By
sharing one electron with a hydrogen atom, both atoms reach the electron
count of the noble gas nearest to them: the chlorine's outer shell fills to 8
— its configuration becomes [2, 8, 8], the same as an argon atom — and the
hydrogen reaches 2 in its outer shell, the same as helium. One shared pair,
one covalent bond, both atoms satisfied. Note that only the **outer-shell**
electrons of chlorine take part: the inner shells ([2, 8]) are spectators,
buried too deep to do any bonding.

That observation sets up the first convention: in the examples you meet at
International GCSE, **inner electrons never get used in bonding**, so they are
usually left out of bonding diagrams entirely. A dot-and-cross diagram for
HCl drawn the standard way shows just the outer shell of chlorine and the
single shell of hydrogen. But — care — this is a convention, not a licence:
**in an exam, only leave out the inner electrons if the question tells you
to** (or shows you it expects outer shells only). If a question asks for all
electrons, draw all of them. Read the question, then choose the drawing.

The second convention: the same bond can be drawn as a **line between the two
atoms** — H–Cl. The line represents one covalent bond (one shared pair).
These line structures are quick and tidy, and you will use them constantly
for organic molecules later in the course. The third convention follows
directly: **a line structure is not a dot-and-cross diagram**. If the
question says "draw a dot-and-cross diagram", a line drawing scores zero even
though the chemistry in it is correct. The examiner is checking the electron
bookkeeping, so the electrons must be on the page.

:::key-point
The HCl diagram teaches the general recipe for every dot-and-cross you will
draw: (1) find each atom's outer-shell electrons from its group number;
(2) pair up the electrons being shared, one origin per atom in the standard
cases; (3) count each atom's outer shell after sharing — 2 for hydrogen,
8 for the others; (4) show only the shells the question asks for. The recipe
is identical for molecules with two atoms or twenty; only the bookkeeping
grows.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Only outer electrons are involved in bonding" is a statement about the
*chemistry*; "only draw outer electrons" is a statement about the *question*.
Keep the two apart. The safe reading habit: look for the phrase "outer shell
electrons only" before you draw anything. If it is there, draw shells-in;
if it is not, draw the full configurations. Half-marks are lost to this
reading slip every session — the diagram is chemically right but answers a
question that was not asked.
:::

:::misconception
"The H–Cl line drawing and the dot-and-cross diagram are the same thing drawn
two ways, so either answers a dot-and-cross question." They carry different
information, and examiners treat them as different answer types. The line
diagram records *that* a bond exists; the dot-and-cross records *where every
outer electron sits and where each came from*. When the question names
dot-and-cross, the electron bookkeeping is the assessed skill — a line
drawing hides exactly what is being marked. Draw lines only when the question
allows or asks for a line structure.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44, 1.45 and 1.46 items — the HCl dot-and-cross
diagram (hydrogen halide, outer shells only), the argon/helium isoelectronic
check on both atoms, and the electrostatic-attraction explanation of what
holds the molecule together. The bank's variant questions flip between
"draw" and "explain what holds the atoms together" so both skills are sharp.
:::

sections.title: Covalent bonding in a chlorine molecule (Cl₂)
sections.markdown:
Two identical atoms can share with each other, and chlorine shows how. A
chlorine atom has 7 electrons in its outer shell — one short of a full octet.
Put two chlorine atoms together and each shares **one** of its electrons with
the other: the shared pair contributes one electron to each atom's count, and
both atoms reach 8 in their outer shells. The result is the Cl₂ molecule — two
chlorine atoms joined by one covalent bond, each atom's outer shell complete.

The diagram has a pleasing symmetry: each atom contributes one electron (one
dot from the left atom, one cross from the right), the pair sits in the
overlap, and each atom also shows its other six outer electrons as its own.
Because the two atoms are identical, there is no question of which atom
"owns" the pair — the sharing is exactly equal, which is why chlorine gas is
made of Cl₂ molecules rather than anything charged. Chlorine is [[diatomic]]
for the same reason hydrogen is: one shared pair completes each atom's outer
shell, and nothing remains to bond with a third atom.

The same diagram can be drawn in more than one way — with the two atoms as
overlapping circles, or with the shared pair written between the chemical
symbols. They are the same chemistry; pick whichever the question asks for.
What never changes is the bookkeeping: 7 + 1 shared = 8, on both sides,
every time.

Chlorine's bonding pattern here generalises to the whole of Group 7: fluorine,
bromine and iodine all have 7 outer electrons and all form the same
single-bonded diatomic molecules — F₂, Br₂, I₂. The group number fixed the
bond count, exactly as the periodic-table work in Chapter 4 (u1:c04) predicts.
Hold on to that prediction skill: group number → outer electrons → bonds
formed → formula of the molecule. The next section applies it to three
molecules at once.

:::exam-hint
"Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for chlorine" is the standard halogen-diagram
question, and the mark scheme checks three things: (1) 7 outer electrons
shown on each atom *before* sharing; (2) exactly one shared pair in the
overlap, one dot + one cross; (3) each atom counting 8 after sharing. Draw
all seven outer electrons per atom — forgetting the six non-bonding ones is
the single most common slip. And if the question says "outer shell electrons
only", do not draw the [2, 8] inner shells at all.
:::

:::misconception
"Two chlorine atoms each share one electron, so the bond contains one
electron." The sharing is of a **pair**: one electron from each atom makes a
two-electron shared pair, and that pair is the bond. Counting the bond as a
single electron wrecks the audit — each atom would land on 7½, which is
nonsense. The safe habit from section 4 applies: after drawing, count each
atom's outer shell in whole electrons (7 own + 1 from the shared pair's other
member = 8) and the error cannot survive.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.44 and 1.46 items — the Cl₂ dot-and-cross diagram
(halogen diatomic, outer shells only) and the group-number-to-bond-count
prediction. The bank rotates the halogens (F₂, Br₂, I₂) through the same
diagram task so the pattern, not the specific atom, is what you learn.
:::

sections.title: Covalent bonding in methane, ammonia and water
sections.markdown:
Three molecules every candidate must be able to draw: methane, ammonia and
water. They are a matched set — a central non-metal atom surrounded by
hydrogen atoms — and drawn one after another they reveal the pattern that
connects the Periodic Table to molecular formulae.

**Methane, CH₄.** A carbon atom has 4 electrons in its outer shell, so it
shares one electron with each of 4 hydrogen atoms: four shared pairs, four
covalent bonds. Count the audit after bonding — the carbon's outer shell
holds 8 (4 of its own plus its share of each pair), and each hydrogen holds
2. The formula CH₄ records the outcome: one carbon bonded to four hydrogens.

**Ammonia, NH₃.** A nitrogen atom has 5 electrons in its outer shell — three
short of 8 — so it shares three of its electrons, one with each of 3 hydrogen
atoms. Three covalent bonds form, and the nitrogen keeps its remaining two
outer electrons as an unshared pair of its own (you will give those a name in
section 10). The audit: N on 8, each H on 2. The formula is NH₃ — three
hydrogens, not four, and the count explains why.

**Water, H₂O.** An oxygen atom has 6 electrons in its outer shell — two short
— so it shares two of its electrons, one with each of 2 hydrogen atoms. Two
covalent bonds, two remaining unshared pairs on the oxygen. The audit: O on
8, each H on 2. The formula H₂O falls straight out of the counting.

Now stand back and read the pattern across the three: carbon (Group 4) formed
**4** bonds, nitrogen (Group 5) formed **3**, oxygen (Group 6) formed **2** —
and chlorine in the last section (Group 7) formed **1**. The number of bonds
a non-metal atom forms is **8 minus its group number** (for Groups 4 to 7),
because each atom bonds until its outer shell reaches 8. That one sentence
generates every formula in this section, and the dot-and-cross diagrams are
just the proof on paper.

:::worked-example
**Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for water, showing outer shells only.**
(1) Oxygen brings 6 outer electrons; hydrogen brings 1 each. (2) Place the
oxygen's electrons around it in pairs; share one oxygen electron with each
hydrogen's single electron — two shared pairs, each shown as a dot+cross
overlap. (3) Draw the oxygen's remaining 4 outer electrons as two unshared
pairs. (4) Audit: O counts 8; each H counts 2. Four marks on the page in
under a minute — and the same four steps draw methane and ammonia with only
the counts changed.
:::

:::exam-hint
The "8 − group number = bonds formed" shortcut earns formulae fast, but in
explain questions the marks live in the *reasoning*: the atom shares until its
outer shell holds 8 (2 for hydrogen). Write the counting sentence, not just
the number. Typical full-mark answer for ammonia: "nitrogen has 5 outer-shell
electrons and needs 3 more to reach 8, so it forms 3 covalent bonds, one with
each of three hydrogen atoms." The same sentence skeleton scores on any
central atom the course can throw at you.
:::

:::misconception
"An atom with 8 outer electrons after bonding must have formed 8 bonds."
Confusing the *target count* with the *number of bonds* is the classic error
on this set. Each covalent bond contributes just one new electron to an
atom's count (its share of the pair), so an atom starting with 5 outer
electrons forms 8 − 5 = 3 bonds — not 8. Audit every diagram by counting, not
by vibes: carbon 4 + 4 bonds, nitrogen 5 + 3, oxygen 6 + 2, chlorine 7 + 1.
The start count is what varies; the target is always 2 or 8.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 items — dot-and-cross diagrams for water,
ammonia and methane (outer shells only) plus the bond-count predictions from
group numbers. The bank shuffles molecule order and asks for both diagram and
explanation, because papers award the marks in exactly that pair.
:::

sections.title: Shapes of molecules
sections.markdown:
Dot-and-cross diagrams are flat, but molecules are not. Understanding the
bonding lets you work out the actual three-dimensional **shape** of a
molecule, and the rule is delightfully simple: **pairs of electrons in the
outer shell of the central atom repel each other, and therefore get as far
apart as possible.**

Take methane. Around the central carbon atom there are four pairs of
electrons — the four shared pairs of the four C–H bonds. All four pairs are
negative and all four repel, so they spread out to the maximum separation
that geometry allows: pointing towards the corners of a **[[tetrahedral]]**
arrangement. A tetrahedron (the noun; "tetrahedral" is the adjective) is a
triangular-based pyramid — one position on top and three around the base.
The carbon sits in the middle and the four hydrogen atoms occupy the four
corners, with bond angles of about 109.5°. Every C–H bond in methane is
identical, so the molecule is a perfectly symmetric spinning top.

Water, from the same rule, cannot be flat either — and it cannot be
tetrahedral *in shape* either, which sounds contradictory until you separate
two ideas: the arrangement of **electron pairs** and the shape formed by the
**atoms**. Water's oxygen also has four electron pairs, and those four also
spread out tetrahedrally — but only two of the pairs are bonds to hydrogen
atoms. The molecule's *atomic* shape is what the two hydrogens and the oxygen
trace out, and you will see in the next section how the other two pairs bend
it into a distinctive V. The electron pairs set the geometry; the atoms show
only part of it.

The prediction recipe, then: count the electron pairs around the central
atom, spread them as far apart as possible, and read off where the *bonded*
atoms sit. Four pairs, all bonding — tetrahedral molecule. Four pairs, two
bonding — bent molecule. The pairs you cannot see in a line drawing are doing
as much geometric work as the bonds you can.

:::cross-curricular
The tetrahedron is a solid you already own from mathematics: a
triangular-based pyramid, one of the Platonic solids, with four triangular
faces. The same solid appears as a fair die with four faces, in the corner
brackets of steel frameworks, and in crystallography — the science of crystal
shapes that grew from exactly this kind of geometry. When chemistry says a
methane molecule is tetrahedral, it is borrowing mathematics' most economical
way of putting four things as far apart as possible in three-dimensional
space: the geometry is not an analogy, it is the same theorem.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two drawing habits score here. First, when drawing organic molecules,
remember that **carbon always forms 4 bonds** (sharing 4 electrons) and
**hydrogen always forms 1** (sharing 1 electron) — and put the **hydrogen
atoms on the outside**, never in the middle of the structure. That single
rule prevents most wrong organic diagrams at this level. Second, in "shape of
molecule" questions, name the arrangement of the electron *pairs* and the
shape of the *atoms* separately: methane's pairs are tetrahedral and so is
its atomic shape; water's pairs are tetrahedral but its atomic shape is bent.
Mixing the two levels loses the marking point.
:::

:::misconception
"A molecule drawn flat on paper is flat in reality." The diagram is a
projection, not a photograph. Methane is drawn as a symmetric flat cross in
simple sketches, but the real molecule is tetrahedral in three dimensions —
no two of those C–H bonds are in the same plane as drawn. When a question
asks about shape, answer from the electron-pair repulsion rule, never from
the flatness of your drawing. The paper is 2D; the chemistry is 3D.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 items — methane as tetrahedral and water as
bent, both justified by electron-pair repulsion around the central atom. The
bank's explain questions supply the marking sentence: "electron pairs repel
and take up positions as far apart as possible." Learn it as a fixed phrase;
it is a marking point nearly verbatim.
:::

sections.title: Water's four electron pairs — lone pairs, bent shapes and polarity
sections.markdown:
Water completes the shape story that section 9 set up. Around the central
oxygen atom there are **four pairs of electrons** — but only two of them are
shared pairs in covalent bonds with the hydrogens. The other two are pairs
that sit on the oxygen's outer shell without bonding to anything: **[[lone-pair]]s** of electrons. All four pairs — bonding and lone alike — repel each
other, so all four adopt the tetrahedral arrangement.

But the *shape of the molecule* is drawn by the atoms, not the pairs. Two of
the four tetrahedral positions are occupied by lone pairs, which show no atom
at all. The oxygen and its two hydrogens therefore trace out only part of the
tetrahedron, and the molecule comes out **bent** — often described as
**V-shaped**. The lone pairs are the hidden scaffolding: invisible in a
formula, decisive in the geometry.

Those lone pairs do something else with a visible consequence. In the O–H
shared pairs, the electrons are attracted **to a different extent** by the
oxygen and by the hydrogen — the oxygen nucleus pulls the shared electrons
towards itself more strongly. Each bond has its electrons shifted slightly
towards the oxygen end, and because the molecule is bent (not symmetric like
methane's spinning top), the little shifts do not cancel. The result: a water
molecule is **[[polar]]** — it has a slightly negative end (towards the
oxygen) and a slightly positive end (towards the hydrogens).

Polarity is not just a label; it is something you can see. A stream of water
from a tap is **bent by an electrically charged object** — run a comb through
dry hair, hold it near a thin trickle of water, and the stream leans towards
the comb. The charged object attracts the slightly charged ends of the water
molecules and pulls the whole stream off course. That demonstration is the
cleanest evidence you will ever see that electron pairs in water are shared
unequally — and it all follows from two unshared pairs and a bent shape.

:::key-point
Lone pairs are electron pairs **in the outer shell of a bonded atom that take
no part in covalent bonding** — but they still repel, still occupy positions
in the arrangement around the central atom, and still count when you work out
a molecule's shape. Water: four pairs total, two bonding, two lone → pairs
tetrahedral, atoms bent. Any shape prediction that ignores lone pairs will
get water wrong.
:::

:::exam-hint
Shape questions about water almost always want the three-step chain: (1) the
oxygen has four electron pairs in its outer shell; (2) the pairs repel and
arrange tetrahedrally; (3) because two pairs are lone pairs, the *molecular*
shape is bent (V-shaped). If the question pushes further — a charged rod
bending a water stream — the marking points are "water is polar" and "the
charged rod attracts the oppositely charged end of the molecule". Write
"lone pairs" by name; papers use the term and so should you.
:::

:::misconception
"Only shared pairs matter, so water should be a straight molecule like
H–O–H on a line." Ignoring the lone pairs deletes half of the oxygen's outer
shell, and the shape prediction collapses. The two lone pairs repel the
bonding pairs exactly as the bonding pairs repel each other — they occupy
their own two corners of the tetrahedron and push the hydrogens together.
The visible result is the bend, and the electrical proof is the comb
experiment. Electron pairs you cannot see still push.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 items — explaining water's bent shape through
the four-pair (two lone, two bonding) arrangement, and linking polarity to
the stream-of-water deflection. The bank's longer questions chain the two:
shape first, consequence second, exactly as the marking schemes sequence the
points.
:::

sections.title: A slightly more complicated molecule — ethane
sections.markdown:
Everything so far had a single central atom. Ethane, C₂H₆, is the first
molecule on the course with **two** carbon atoms, and it is your bridge from
simple inorganic diagrams to the organic molecules of Unit 4 — built from
nothing but the rules you already have.

Start from methane and extend it. In methane, one carbon shares with four
hydrogens. In ethane, each of the two carbon atoms bonds to **three**
hydrogen atoms — and the two carbons bond **to each other**, each contributing
one electron to a shared pair in the C–C bond. Run the audit atom by atom:
each carbon has 4 outer electrons, spends 3 sharing with hydrogens and 1
sharing with the other carbon, and ends with 8; each hydrogen shares one pair
and ends with 2. Six C–H bonds and one C–C bond — seven covalent bonds in
total, and every atom on 2-or-8. The formula C₂H₆ is the diagram's summary.

The drawing strategy for any two-carbon molecule is now on the table: draw
the carbon–carbon connection first, then hang the hydrogens off each carbon
until every carbon's count reaches 8. Hydrogens go on the outside (section
9's rule), each carrying its single shared pair. No new bonding ideas are
needed — only careful bookkeeping with more atoms on the page.

Ethane is also your first explicitly **organic compound**: a compound built
around carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonding. There is a whole unit of
this ahead (Unit 4, from u4:c22 onwards) — fuels, alcohols, polymers — and
every one of those molecules will be drawn with exactly the technique you
just used. Nothing about organic chemistry at this level is a new bonding
theory; it is the same shared pairs, in bigger and more interesting
arrangements.

:::exam-hint
When a question asks for the dot-and-cross diagram of ethane (outer electrons
only), the fastest safe order is: (1) place the two carbon atoms side by side
and share a pair between them (one dot, one cross) for the C–C bond;
(2) attach three hydrogens to *each* carbon, each sharing one pair;
(3) fill each carbon's remaining outer electrons; (4) audit — each carbon on
8, each hydrogen on 2, seven bonds total. Carbon-4-bonds, hydrogen-1-bond,
hydrogens-on-the-outside: the three-part rule from section 9 does all the
work.
:::

:::misconception
"Ethane is two methane molecules joined together." Molecules do not join to
make bigger molecules by sticking — ethane is one molecule with one specific
bonding arrangement: two carbons sharing a pair directly with each other, and
three hydrogens per carbon. The phrase "two methanes" also gets the bonding
wrong at the joint: a C–C shared pair is a genuine covalent bond with its own
two electrons, not a kind of staple between two finished CH₄ units. Draw the
C–C shared pair explicitly and the distinction draws itself.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 items — the ethane dot-and-cross diagram
(two-carbon organic molecule, outer shells only) and the atom-by-atom 2-or-8
audit. The bank pairs ethane with methane so the extension pattern
(methane → ethane by sharing carbons) is the transferable skill you drill.
:::

sections.title: Multiple covalent bonding — double and triple bonds
sections.markdown:
Atoms are not limited to sharing one pair between them. When sharing one
pair is not enough to complete both outer shells, they share **two** or even
**three** pairs — and these multiple bonds are among the most examined
diagrams on the course.

**The double bond: oxygen, O₂.** An oxygen atom has 6 electrons in its outer
shell — two short of 8. If two oxygen atoms each shared just one electron,
both would still be one short. So they share **two electrons each**, giving
**two shared pairs** between the atoms: a **[[double-bond]]** (or double
covalent bond). Count the audit: each oxygen counts 6 own + 2 from its share
of the two pairs = 8. Two shared pairs, four electrons, one very strong bond
— and O₂ is the molecule that runs your respiration on exactly this
arrangement.

**The double bond in carbon dioxide, CO₂.** A carbon atom has 4 outer
electrons; an oxygen atom has 6. Each oxygen shares two electrons with the
carbon, and the carbon shares two with each oxygen: **two double bonds**, one
from the carbon to each oxygen. Every atom lands on 8 — carbon on 8 via its
two double bonds, each oxygen on 8 via its one. The line structure is O=C=O,
two double bonds in a row; the dot-and-cross shows the four shared pairs
explicitly, two per bond.

**The triple bond: nitrogen, N₂.** A nitrogen atom has 5 outer electrons —
three short. Two nitrogen atoms each share **three** electrons, giving three
shared pairs: a **[[triple-bond]]**. Each atom counts 5 + 3 = 8. The triple
bond in N₂ is **very strong and needs a lot of energy to break**, and that
single sentence of structure explains a headline chemical fact: **nitrogen gas
is relatively unreactive**. The air is four-fifths nitrogen, and it stays
chemically sleepy precisely because its molecules are held together by three
shared pairs apiece. Structure → strength → unreactivity: one line of
reasoning, three marking points.

**The double bond in ethene, C₂H₄.** Ethene is rather like ethane except
that each carbon has only **two** hydrogen atoms attached, and the two
carbons make up the difference with a **double bond between them**. Each
carbon: two C–H single bonds plus one C=C double bond — 2 + 2 shared pairs
= 8. You will meet ethene again as the starting material for polymers
(u4:c25); the bonding you would draw for it here is the same diagram.

:::worked-example
**Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for CO₂, outer electrons only.** (1) Carbon
brings 4 outer electrons; each oxygen brings 6. (2) Between C and each O,
place **two** shared pairs (two dot–cross overlaps per bond) — that is
carbons' 4 electrons all shared, two to each oxygen. (3) Draw each oxygen's
remaining 4 electrons as two lone pairs. (4) Audit: C on 8 (its share of four
pairs), each O on 8 (its share of two pairs plus its own four). If any atom
misses 8, the bond order — not the atom — is what you mis-set.
:::

:::exam-hint
Ethane and ethene are **completely different compounds** — a single letter
apart in their names, worlds apart in their bonding (seven single bonds
versus six bonds including a C=C double). In every organic-naming question,
read the name letter by letter before drawing anything: -ane means single
bonds throughout; -ene means a C=C double bond is present. Papers love this
pair precisely because fast readers draw the wrong molecule. The same care
applies to the formulae: C₂H₆ and C₂H₄ differ by two hydrogens, and those two
hydrogens are the double bond's other face.
:::

:::misconception
"A double bond is two separate single bonds drawn side by side, so the atoms
share with each other twice as many *times*." A double bond is **two shared
pairs between the same two atoms** — one bond made of four shared electrons,
not two independent bonds to two different atoms. The audit keeps it honest:
O₂'s oxygens each count 8 total, not 8 twice. The mirror error appears in
counts: "a double bond counts as two bonds for the atom's 8" is right, but
"a double bond gives each atom four extra electrons" is wrong — each atom
gains only its share, two electrons, from either a double bond's two pairs
(two electrons each) or two single bonds. Count electrons, not bond labels.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 items — dot-and-cross diagrams for O₂, N₂ and
CO₂ (diatomic + inorganic molecules with multiple bonds, outer shells only),
plus the explanation chain "N₂ has a triple bond → very strong → needs much
energy to break → nitrogen is relatively unreactive". The bank's hardest
variants make you pick bond order from the atom counts alone.
:::

sections.title: Organic molecules containing halogen atoms
sections.markdown:
Real organic molecules mix their atoms, and the exam's favourite mixture is a
carbon–hydrogen skeleton with a halogen (Group 7) atom attached. Two
molecules cover every rule you need.

**Bromomethane, CH₃Br.** Three hydrogen atoms and one bromine atom are joined
to a central carbon atom. You might worry about the bromine: with 35
electrons in total, you have never worked out its full electronic
configuration — and you do not need to. Look at the Periodic Table: bromine
sits in **Group 7**, so it has **7 electrons in its outer shell**, and it will
share 1 electron to reach 8. Therefore bromine forms **exactly 1 covalent
bond**, just as chlorine did in HCl and Cl₂. The diagram for CH₃Br shows
**outer shells only**: carbon on 8 (three C–H pairs plus one C–Br pair), each
hydrogen on 2, bromine on 8 with its three lone pairs drawn in. The rule that
saves you: **the group number gives the outer electrons; you never need the
inner ones** — and in diagrams you are only asked for outer electrons anyway.
(Colours are a drawing convenience, not chemistry: examiners accept any
clearly labelled dot-and-cross, in one colour or many.)

**Chloroethene, CH₂CHCl.** Probably the most complicated molecule for which
you could be asked to draw a dot-and-cross at this level — and it is just two
rules stacked. Each carbon forms 4 bonds; each hydrogen forms 1; the chlorine
(Group 7) forms 1. The two carbons are bonded to each other, each carrying
two hydrogens except where the substitution sits: one carbon holds two H's
and the other holds one H plus the Cl. Count to check the double bond: each
carbon has 4 electrons to share; after its hydrogens (and the Cl on the
second carbon), the leftover electron on each carbon pairs up between the
carbons — giving the C=C **double bond** between them. The audit: both
carbons on 8, hydrogens on 2, chlorine on 8 with three lone pairs.

One trap to disarm: the same molecule can be drawn as a dot-and-cross diagram
*or* as a line structure showing the bonds — and they are **different
answers to different questions**. The line structure is quicker, but if the
question asks for a dot-and-cross diagram, the electrons must appear as dots
and crosses with their shared pairs visible. Choose by the question's words,
not by which drawing you prefer.

:::key-point
Extension — atoms in Period 3 and below can break the octet ceiling. The
maximum number of electrons a central atom can **share** equals the number of
electrons in its outer shell. Sulfur (6 outer electrons) can form up to **6
bonds** — as in SF₆ — and chlorine (7) can form up to **7**, as in HClO₄.
Outer atoms still finish on 8; only generous central atoms grow beyond it.
You will not be asked to draw these heavyweights often, but knowing they
exist stops you from "correcting" a right diagram into a wrong one.
:::

:::exam-hint
For every halogenated organic molecule: identify each atom's bond count
**from its group** before drawing — C (Group 4) 4 bonds; H 1; Cl, Br, I
(Group 7) 1 bond each with three lone pairs left over. Then let the bond
counts *generate* the structure: in CH₂CHCl the counts force the C=C double
bond, because two carbons with only three substituents each have one electron
left over to share with each other. Questions hand you the formula; the group
numbers hand you the diagram.
:::

:::misconception
"I can't draw bromomethane because I don't know bromine's full electronic
configuration." This stalls more candidates than any chemistry in the
chapter. Full configurations are irrelevant to outer-shell diagrams: a
Group 7 atom has 7 outer electrons and forms 1 bond, whether it is chlorine
with 17 electrons or iodine with 53. The Periodic Table position *is* the
information. If you catch yourself counting inner shells to reach a halogen,
stop — the group number already answered the question.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 items — dot-and-cross diagrams for
halogen-containing organic molecules up to two carbons (bromomethane,
chloroethene), outer shells only. The bank drills the group-number
bond-count reasoning as a written marking point alongside the diagram, since
papers ask "how many bonds does bromine form and why?" as often as they ask
for the picture.
:::

sections.title: Difficult molecules — when the central atom does not have 8 electrons
sections.markdown:
The 2-or-8 rule is strong but not universal, and the exceptions are
examinable. The reliable part first: **outer atoms** in a molecule will
virtually always finish with 8 outer electrons (or 2 for hydrogen). The
flexible part: a few **central atoms** finish with more or fewer than 8. Two
molecules cover both directions.

**Fewer than 8: boron trifluoride, BF₃.** Boron is the central atom with the
three fluorines around it. Each fluorine (Group 7) shares 1 electron to reach
8 — that part is untouched. But boron only has **3 electrons in its outer
shell**, and 3 is the maximum it can share. After three B–F bonds, boron's
outer shell holds just **6 electrons**. It cannot do better: an atom cannot
share electrons it does not have. BF₃ is therefore a stable, real molecule
with an incomplete central octet — the count *predicts* it, and no amount of
insisting on "8" will draw it away.

**More than 8: sulfur dioxide, SO₂** (also called sulfur(IV) oxide). Sulfur
sits central with two oxygens around it. Each oxygen (Group 6) needs to share
2 electrons to reach 8, so the sulfur shares 2 electrons with each oxygen —
**two double bonds**. But a sulfur atom starts with 6 outer electrons, and
now it is sharing 4 of them: after bonding it has **10 electrons in its outer
shell**. Ten — past the octet, and perfectly stable. The pattern across both
examples: the *outer* atoms always get their 8; the *central* atom ends up
with whatever its own electron supply and bond demand produce. When you draw,
count the central atom honestly rather than forcing it to 8.

The same page of the chapter also plants a term that the rest of this lesson
depends on. **[[intermolecular-forces]]** — the name is literal:
*inter*-molecular, **between molecules**. Water evaporating and boiling gives
the picture: only the forces *between* the water molecules are broken when
liquid water becomes steam — every molecule's internal covalent bonds ride
along intact. Keep the two scales apart in your head: covalent bonds *inside*
molecules (strong, not broken on boiling), intermolecular forces *between*
molecules (weak, broken on boiling). Sections 15 and 16 turn that separation
into the melting-point story, and spec 1.47 names it directly.

If you continue chemistry beyond International GCSE you will find that
"intermolecular forces" is an umbrella for several distinct mechanisms — you
will meet names such as van der Waals' forces, London dispersion forces and
hydrogen bonds. One of them is already visible in your own kitchen: water has
a special intermolecular force called **hydrogen bonding**, and it gives
water some of its very unusual properties — including the fact that ice, the
solid form, is *less* dense than liquid water, so ice floats. At this level
"intermolecular forces" as a single term is all you need; the plumbing behind
it comes later.

:::exam-hint
Do not force the octet onto central atoms. If your BF₃ diagram shows boron on
6 — three bonds, no lone pairs to add — leave it there: that is the correct
diagram, and "boron has only 3 outer electrons to share" is the explaining
sentence the mark scheme wants. Likewise SO₂'s sulfur sits on 10, and
"sulfur shares 4 electrons so it has 10 in its outer shell" is the matching
point. Auditing an *outer* atom short of 8 means your diagram is wrong;
finding a *central* atom off 8 may simply mean you drew one of this section's
molecules correctly.
:::

:::misconception
"Every atom in every molecule must end with exactly 8 outer electrons, so BF₃
cannot exist and SO₂ must be wrong." The 8 rule describes the overwhelmingly
common case, not a law of chemistry. Boron ends on 6 because it has only 3
electrons to give; sulfur ends on 10 because its bonds demand more sharing
than 8 allows. The invariant that *never* breaks: outer atoms reach 8 (2 for
hydrogen). Draw from the electron counts and let the central number land
where it lands.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.46 and 1.47 items — the BF₃ and SO₂ diagrams
(central atoms on 6 and 10) and the meaning of "intermolecular forces" as the
forces *between* molecules. The bank's discriminating question shows a
correct BF₃ diagram and asks what is wrong with it — the honest answer is
"nothing", and defending that answer is the skill.
:::

sections.title: Simple molecular structures
sections.markdown:
Molecules contain fixed numbers of atoms joined by **strong covalent bonds**
— but that is only the inside story. Look closely at a glass of liquid water:
there are individual water molecules, each with its H and O atoms locked
together covalently. Yet the water sits in the glass rather than flying apart
as gas, so something must be holding the molecules *to each other*. That
something is the [[intermolecular-forces]] from section 14 — weak attractions
between neighbouring molecules.

The scale comparison is the whole of this section in one sentence:
**intermolecular forces are much, much weaker than covalent bonds.** Strong
inside each molecule; weak between neighbouring molecules. A substance made
of molecules with intermolecular forces between them has a **[[simple-molecular-structure]]** — and virtually every covalent compound you have met
in this lesson has one: H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃, C₂H₄ — exactly the molecules you
drew dot-and-cross diagrams for.

Now the consequence that examiners ask about every year. When you boil
water, **only the weak intermolecular forces break — the covalent bonds do
not.** Steam is still H₂O: the same bent molecules, same two O–H covalent
bonds per molecule, same electron-pair sharing. All that has changed is the
separation — the molecules have torn free of one another, because it takes
only a little energy to snap the weak attractions between them. Nobody has
split a single O–H bond, which is why boiling is a physical change and why
the steam condenses straight back to water when it cools: covalent bonds were
never touched, so nothing chemical ever happened.

Flip the same reasoning to the melting and boiling points themselves.
Because so little energy is needed to break the weak intermolecular forces,
**substances with simple molecular structures tend to be gases, liquids, or
solids with low melting points and low boiling points.** Methane boils at a
frigid −162 °C; carbon dioxide sublimes at −78 °C; even room-temperature
liquids like ethanol boil well under 200 °C. The covalent bonds inside the
molecules are as strong as ever — they are simply *not the forces being
tested* when the substance melts or boils. Keep the two force types labelled
in your answer and the explanation writes itself.

:::key-point
The single most examined distinction in this chapter: when a simple molecular
substance **melts or boils, only the weak intermolecular forces of attraction
break. The covalent bonds inside the molecules never break.** Steam is still
H₂O; gaseous methane is still CH₄. Every "explain the low boiling point"
mark scheme awards its points for exactly this separation — weak forces
broken (little energy) versus strong covalent bonds intact.
:::

:::exam-hint
The question "what is broken when water boils?" has one right answer and a
famous wrong one. Right: **intermolecular forces of attraction between the
molecules**. Wrong: the covalent O–H bonds. The wrong answer is also the
 chemically absurd one — if boiling split water's covalent bonds, the steam
would be hydrogen and oxygen gases, not steam. Structure-and-bonding papers
use this exact test on both water and hydrocarbons; write "intermolecular
forces between molecules are broken, covalent bonds within the molecules are
not" and bank all the marks.
:::

:::misconception
"When water boils, the molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen." If that
were true, boiling would be a chemical reaction and steam would be two new
substances. It is not: the molecules survive boiling completely intact, and
the gas is still H₂O — just molecules that have escaped from each other. The
energy went into overcoming the weak attractions *between* molecules, which
is a physical change, reversible with no chemistry at all. Molecules move
apart when boiled; they do not come apart.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.47 items — defining simple molecular structure and
explaining why such substances are gases, liquids or low-melting solids
(weak intermolecular forces need little energy; covalent bonds remain
unbroken). The bank's marking points mirror spec 1.47's own wording —
practise the explanation against both the "why low mp/bp" and "what breaks
on boiling" framings.
:::

sections.title: Melting and boiling points increase as relative molecular mass increases
sections.markdown:
Section 15 said molecular substances melt and boil easily. This section
refines the rule into a trend you can predict — the trend spec 1.48 is built
on — using the halogens as its cleanest evidence.

The halogens (Group 7) all have simple molecular structures: [[diatomic]]
molecules with intermolecular forces between them. Line up the group and read
their numbers:

| Halogen | Formula | Relative molecular mass (Mᵣ) | Melting point / °C | Boiling point / °C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fluorine | F₂ | 38 | −220 | −188 |
| chlorine | Cl₂ | 71 | −101 | −34 |
| bromine | Br₂ | 160 | −7 | 59 |
| iodine | I₂ | 254 | 114 | 184 |

The trend is unmissable: **as the relative molecular mass increases, the
melting points and boiling points increase.** Fluorine is a gas at room
temperature, chlorine a gas just above it, bromine a liquid, iodine a grey
solid — the same room, four states, ordered by molecular mass alone. (Note
the iodine data point in particular: a molecular substance that is a *solid*
at room temperature — "molecular" does not have to mean "gas".)

The *why* is an energy argument you already own. To melt or boil one of these
substances you must break [[intermolecular-forces]] — no covalent bonds. Higher
boiling points mean more energy must be put in, which means the
**intermolecular forces must be getting stronger** as the relative molecular
mass rises. Bigger molecules attract their neighbours more strongly; bigger
Mᵣ, stickier neighbours, higher temperatures needed to pull them apart. The
same trend walks up the alkane series — methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane
(C₃H₈) boil at steadily higher temperatures as Mᵣ grows — and you will meet
that family properly in Chapter 23 (u4:c23).

Two pieces of fine print make your answer examiner-proof. First, the
vocabulary: a covalent compound with a simple molecular structure is called a
**covalent molecular compound** — the pairing of terms that papers use when
they want precision. Second, the honesty: the trend is stated "in general"
because it strictly holds only within families of similar substances — the
halogens, the alkanes. Across the whole of chemistry it leaks: water (Mᵣ 18)
boils at 100 °C while ethane (Mᵣ 30) boils at −89 °C, and ammonia (Mᵣ 17)
beats phosphine (Mᵣ 34) by over 120 degrees. The anomalies come from
especially strong intermolecular attractions in water and ammonia — a hint of
hydrogen bonding from section 14. Trend first, exceptions second: that is
the order the marks are written in.

:::key-point
A tetrahedron is a triangular-based pyramid, and a **tetrahedral arrangement**
puts one atom at the centre with four atoms at the corners. You will meet the
shape again built in three dimensions when the chapter reaches diamond — and
when a structure diagram shows a carbon atom apparently bonded to only two
others, read the caption's caution: diagrams of giant structures show a small
slice of something that continues in all directions, and every atom drawn is
bonded to four neighbours in the full structure. Diagram edges are not
chemistry.
:::

:::maths-skills
Reading the halogen table is a data-handling skill papers test directly.
Describe the trend with **both variables named and both directions fixed**:
"as relative molecular mass increases from 38 (F₂) to 254 (I₂), the melting
point increases from −220 °C to 114 °C". Quote *both* ends of the range —
an answer with numbers from the table outscores a bare "it increases". And
watch the negative values: iodine's melting point (114 °C) is *higher* than
fluorine's (−220 °C) even though 114 < 220 in absolute terms; on a
temperature scale, less negative means higher. Papers deliberately include
negative melting points to test exactly this reading.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why the boiling point increases down Group 7" — the full-mark chain
has three links and they must all appear: (1) the molecules are held together
by intermolecular forces; (2) as relative molecular mass increases the
intermolecular forces become **stronger**; (3) so **more energy** is needed
to break them, giving higher boiling points. The classic wrong answer names
covalent bonds — "bigger molecules have stronger covalent bonds, so they are
harder to separate". Zero marks: covalent bonds are not broken on boiling,
and stronger covalent bonds would change nothing about the boiling point at
all.
:::

:::misconception
"Higher melting and boiling points mean the covalent bonds inside the
molecules are getting stronger." The property being measured tests the forces
*between* molecules, not the bonds *within* them — I₂'s covalent I–I bond is
no stronger than F₂'s F–F bond to any relevant degree, yet iodine melts 334
degrees higher. What grows down the group is the intermolecular attraction,
because heavier molecules with more electrons attract their neighbours more
strongly. If your explanation of a melting-point trend names covalent bonds,
you have answered about the wrong force — switch to intermolecular forces and
the marks reappear.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.47 and 1.48 items — the Mᵣ-versus-boiling-point
trend, the "intermolecular forces strengthen as relative molecular mass
increases" mechanism, and the data-reading questions built on the halogen
table. The bank includes the deliberate distractor ("stronger covalent
bonds") so you learn to route around it as reliably as the examiner plants it.
:::

sections.title: Some other physical properties of covalent compounds
sections.markdown:
Melting and boiling are not the only properties that follow from structure.
Covalent molecular substances carry a signature across conductivity and
solubility too — and the reasoning is the same structure-first method you
have practised all lesson.

**Conductivity: no.** Covalent molecular compounds **do not conduct
electricity**. Two conditions must hold before anything conducts: there must
be charged particles, and they must be **free to move**. Molecular substances
fail on both counts. The molecules carry **no overall electrical charge**
(there are no ions — sharing is not charging), and all the electrons are held
tightly: locked in atoms or fixed in covalent bonds between specific atoms,
**unable to move from molecule to molecule**. No mobile charges, no current —
pure water, candle wax, sugar and hexane are all insulators, and the reason
is the same in every case.

**Solubility in water: usually no.** Covalent molecular substances **tend to
be insoluble in water**. Water is a polar solvent (section 10) and most
molecular substances do not interact with it strongly enough to be pulled
apart into solution. The exceptions are instructive rather than
embarrassing: **ethanol** (C₂H₅OH) mixes with water in any proportion, and
substances such as **ammonia** and **hydrogen chloride** dissolve readily —
because they **react with water** as they dissolve, forming new species. A
reaction-driven "dissolving" is chemistry, not just mixing; that is why HCl
in water is hydrochloric acid, a new substance entirely.

**Solubility in organic solvents: usually yes.** The mirror image: covalent
molecular substances are **often soluble in organic solvents** — liquids such
as ethanol, propanone (nail-varnish remover) and hexane. Like dissolves
like: molecular solutes sit happily among molecular solvents. This is the
working rule behind everyday chemistry — nail varnish (molecular) dissolves
in propanone (molecular) but not in water; grease dissolves in petrol but not
in rain.

Put the three properties beside the melting-point rule from sections 15–16
and the molecular profile is complete: low melting and boiling points, no
conductivity, water-insoluble but organic-solvent-soluble. Contrast the ionic
profile from Chapter 7 (u1:c07) — high melting points, conducting when molten
or dissolved. Every question in this family is answered by asking one thing:
*what particles are present, and can they move?*

:::exam-hint
Conductivity explanations are marked by the **two-part test**: (1) there are
no charged particles (no ions) / the molecules are neutral, and (2) the
electrons are held tightly in atoms and covalent bonds and **cannot move from
molecule to molecule**. Write both parts — "no free to move charge carriers"
alone is often only half the marks. And when the paper sets a table of
substances and asks which conducts, run the ionic/covalent classification
first (that is the chapter-questions skill too): molecular → no.
:::

:::misconception
"Covalent substances never conduct — full stop, no explanation needed." The
conclusion is right at this level (spec 1.51 says "not usually") but the
unexplained version scores one mark at best. Equally dangerous is the
invented mechanism: "they conduct a little because the molecules move". Fixed
molecules moving around does not make a current — a current is **charge
carriers moving**, and molecules are neutral. Learn the proper two-part
mechanism once (no ions, electrons locked in bonds) and deploy it in every
answer; the property is the conclusion, the particles are the marks.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.51 items — why covalent molecular compounds do not
usually conduct electricity, in the two-part marking language (neutral
molecules / no mobile charged particles). The bank cross-references the ionic
conductivity answers from u1:c07 so the contrast — ions free to move versus
nothing free to move — becomes a single retrievable frame.
:::

sections.title: Giant covalent structures — diamond
sections.markdown:
Everything molecular so far shared one feature: the covalent bonds stopped at
the edge of each molecule. Now meet the substances where the covalent bonds
**never stop** — and discover why the same shared pairs that build methane
also build the hardest natural material on Earth.

**Diamond is a form of pure carbon.** Each carbon atom has four electrons in
its outer shell, so — by the rule you have used all lesson — it forms **four
covalent bonds**. In diamond, each carbon atom bonds strongly to **four other
carbon atoms** arranged tetrahedrally around it (section 9's shape, made
physical). Each of those neighbours bonds to four more, and so on outward
without end: the covalent bonds continue **on and on in three dimensions**
through the entire crystal. This is a **[[giant-covalent-structure]]** — a
structure, not a molecule.

That last point is worth its own paragraph because it is a favourite
examiner trap. Diamond is **not a molecule**, because molecules always
contain a *fixed* number of atoms, and the number of atoms joined together in
a real diamond **is completely variable — it depends on the size of the
crystal**. A tiny diamond and a huge one are chemically identical but contain
different numbers of atoms, so no formula like "C₂₅₀" could ever describe
one. The carbon-to-carbon ratio is always 1:1 (the substance is pure carbon),
but there is no molecule to count. Compare: methane is always CH₄, exactly;
diamond is just... carbon, extended.

**Melting and boiling: very high.** To melt diamond you must break the very
strong carbon–carbon covalent bonds, and those bonds extend **throughout the
whole crystal in three dimensions** — there is no weak seam anywhere. A
tremendous amount of energy has to be supplied, so diamond has very high
melting and boiling points. Feel the contrast with the molecular story from
sections 15–16: to melt methane you only had to nudge molecules apart from
weak intermolecular attractions; to melt diamond you have to *unbuild the
covalent network itself*. Same bonding principle, opposite energy bill — and
that contrast **is** spec 1.49 and spec 1.47 sitting side by side on the
paper.

**Hardness: extreme.** The same structure explains it. A lot of energy is
needed to break the strong covalent bonds in the giant structure, so diamond
is **very hard — the hardest naturally occurring substance** — and crystalline.
That is not trivia: drill bits for stone and rock are **tipped with
diamonds**, because nothing else holds its edge against rock.

:::key-point
"Giant" in chemistry has a precise meaning: the structure **continues in
three dimensions with no fixed limit** — no molecule, no fixed atom count,
no edge formula. Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide (SiO₂) are the course's
three giant covalent structures. Any sentence that calls diamond a "molecule"
or gives it a molecular formula has already lost the marking point; the right
vocabulary is *structure*, *network*, *crystal*, *giant covalent*.
:::

:::exam-hint
The 4-mark giant-covalent explanation has a fixed skeleton worth memorising:
(1) each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds to four other carbon atoms;
(2) the strong covalent bonds extend throughout the giant structure in three
dimensions; (3) a large amount of energy is needed to break them; (4)
therefore diamond has a very high melting point / is very hard. Papers ask
the same chain for melting point, hardness, and "why is diamond different
from methane?" — one skeleton, three question skins. Notice what is *never*
in the answer: intermolecular forces. Diamond has none (no molecules!).
:::

:::misconception
"Diamond is one enormous molecule." The error is understandable — it is one
connected object — but "molecule" means a *fixed* number of atoms, and a
diamond's atom count is whatever the crystal's size makes it. Two diamonds
differ in atom count while being the same substance; no molecule behaves that
way. Say **giant covalent structure** and you keep the marking points; say
"molecule" and you contradict the definition the examiner is testing. The
same warning applies in reverse to methane: it is a genuine molecule because
its atom count is fixed at 5, every time.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.49 items — explaining why giant covalent
structures are solids with high melting and boiling points (strong covalent
bonds throughout the 3D network; much energy to break). The bank pairs
diamond with the molecular substances from sections 15–16 so the two energy
stories — weak forces versus strong network bonds — stay sharply separated.
:::

sections.title: Graphite, fullerene — and the chapter close
sections.markdown:
One idea remains to complete the giant-covalent picture, and then the
chapter's strangest twist: two more forms of carbon that break every
generalisation diamond just set up.

First, close diamond's file properly. When you melt a molecular substance you
break the relatively weak [[intermolecular-forces]] — but **diamond has no
intermolecular forces at all**, because it has no molecules. Melting it means
breaking covalent bonds, which are very strong, and that is the whole reason
for the enormous temperatures. Generalise it: **all substances with giant
covalent structures are solids with high melting and boiling points**, because
a lot of energy is needed to break the strong covalent bonds running through
the entire structure. Diamond's companions on the course are **graphite** and
**silicon dioxide (SiO₂)** — sand. Two more diamond facts worth carrying: it
does not dissolve in water or any other solvent (those strong bonds would
have to break), and it **conducts heat better than any other element** — heat
one end and the vibrations race along the strong bonds to the other.

**Diamond does not conduct electricity.** Every outer-shell electron of every
carbon atom is tightly held in a covalent bond between specific atoms — none
are free to move, so there is nothing to carry a current. Keep that fact warm:
graphite, made of the very same carbon atoms, is about to break this rule,
and the contrast is one of the most examined comparisons in the course.

**Graphite is also pure carbon — with the atoms arranged differently.** It is
still a giant structure, but layered rather than fully three-dimensional:
picture a **pack of playing cards**. Within each "card" (layer), carbon atoms
are bonded by strong covalent bonds; between the cards, only weak attractions
hold the layers together. Within each layer, each carbon atom is bonded to
only **three** neighbours, not four.

That "only three" is the whole story of graphite's electrical fame. Each
carbon uses three of its four outer electrons for its three bonds — and the
**fourth electron is free to move throughout the whole layer**. Electrons
that move freely through a structure like this are called **[[delocalised-electron]]**, and their movement is exactly what carries a current: **graphite
conducts electricity**. Diamond and graphite — same element, same shared-pair
bonding, opposite conductivity — because in diamond every electron is
committed to a bond, while in graphite one electron per atom is left over and
mobile.

**Graphite is soft and slippery** — for the mirror-image reason. The bonds
*within* each layer are very strong, but the attractions *between* layers are
much weaker, so the layers slide over each other and flake apart with little
effort. When you write with a pencil, you are leaving a trail of graphite
layers behind on the paper (pencil "lead" is graphite mixed with clay for
hardness). Pure graphite is so slippery that powdered graphite is used as a
**dry lubricant** — in locks, for instance. (A refinement for the curious:
graphite's slipperiness actually depends on water molecules sticking between
the layers — graphite is not a lubricant in a vacuum.) Yet graphite still has
**high melting and boiling points**: to melt it you must break up the whole
layered structure, including the strong covalent bonds — weak inter-layer
attractions alone do not melt it. It is also insoluble in everything (too many
strong bonds to break) and **less dense than diamond**, because the gaps
between its layers are more than twice the atomic spacing within a layer — a
graphite crystal is, in a sense, full of wasted space that diamond does not
have.

**And now the third form of carbon.** Different fullerenes exist, whose
molecules contain different numbers of carbon atoms — which is why the name
carries a number: **C₆₀ fullerene** is a molecule containing exactly **60
carbon atoms** joined by covalent bonds, arranged as a hollow ball. Here is
the twist: diamond and graphite have giant structures, but C₆₀ fullerene has
a **[[simple-molecular-structure]]** — discrete molecules, weak
intermolecular forces between them. That structural difference rebuilds every
property: C₆₀ has **lower melting and boiling points** than diamond and
graphite (melting it breaks only the weak intermolecular forces, not covalent
bonds); it **dissolves in some solvents** (again, only weak forces to break —
unlike the insoluble giants); and it **does not conduct electricity**. Each
of its carbons forms three bonds like graphite's, but the fourth electron can
only move around *within its own C₆₀ molecule* — electrons cannot jump from
molecule to molecule, so no charge can flow through the solid. One element,
three arrangements, three property profiles: structure decides everything.

Diamond, graphite and C₆₀ fullerene are **[[allotrope]]s** — different forms
of the same element in the same physical state. The allotrope idea will
return with oxygen and ozone, and with sulfur; the carbon trio is where you
learned it.

:::key-point
A **[[delocalised-electron]]** is an outer-shell electron that belongs to no
single bond and can move through the structure — in graphite, the fourth
electron of every carbon, mobile within its layer. Delocalised electrons are
the charge carriers that make graphite conduct. Use the word *delocalised*:
unqualified phrasings about electrons being loose or roaming at liberty are
marked imprecise, and in structure-and-bonding answers the correct term is
itself a marking point.
:::

:::exam-hint
The four-way comparison — diamond, graphite, C₆₀ fullerene and a molecular
substance — is this chapter's classic 6-marker. Organise every answer by
**structure → particles → forces → property**: diamond (giant covalent; strong
bonds throughout; high mp/bp, hard, no conductivity), graphite (giant layered;
delocalised electrons per layer; conducts, soft between layers, high mp/bp),
C₆₀ (simple molecular; weak forces between molecules; low mp/bp, soluble in
some solvents, no conductivity). Practise writing the graphite-conductivity
paragraph and the C₆₀-non-conductivity paragraph back to back — papers ask
them as a pair precisely to catch candidates who memorised one carbon form
and pattern-matched the rest.
:::

:::misconception
"Graphite is soft, so its covalent bonds must be weak." The softness belongs
to the *gaps between layers*, not the bonds within them — within a layer the
C–C bonds are as strong as diamond's, which is exactly why graphite still
needs enormous temperatures to melt and why it is insoluble. The two
properties point at two different forces: sliding tests the weak
inter-layer attractions; melting and dissolving test the strong covalent
bonds. Candidates who write "weak bonds in graphite" lose the melting-point
mark that the same question always carries.
:::

:::summary
The chapter in four movements: **(1) The covalent bond** — a shared pair of
electrons, held by electrostatic attraction between the pair and both nuclei
(1.44, 1.45). **(2) Drawing it** — dot-and-cross diagrams, outer shells only,
for H₂, HCl, Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, O₂, N₂, CO₂, ethane, ethene and halogen
molecules; 2 electrons for hydrogen, 8 for the rest, with named exceptions
(BF₃ on 6, SO₂ on 10); shapes from electron-pair repulsion (1.46). **(3) The
molecular story** — weak intermolecular forces between molecules break on
melting and boiling (covalent bonds never do), so molecular substances melt
and boil low, with the trend rising as relative molecular mass rises; no
conductivity, usually water-insoluble (1.47, 1.48, 1.51). **(4) The giant
counter-story** — diamond, graphite and SiO₂ build covalent bonds
continuously in three dimensions: high melting and boiling points; and the
carbon allotropes show structure deciding everything — diamond hard and
insulating, graphite soft and conducting via delocalised electrons, C₆₀
molecular and low-melting (1.49, 1.50).
:::

:::can-you
Tick each of these before you call the chapter done — they are the eight
objectives in the words examiners use:

- state that a covalent bond is a **shared pair of electrons**, and explain
  the bond as electrostatic attraction between the pair and both nuclei?
- draw **dot-and-cross diagrams** (outer shells only) for H₂, HCl, Cl₂, H₂O,
  CH₄, NH₃, O₂, N₂, CO₂, ethane, ethene and a halogen-containing organic
  molecule — and audit every atom to 2-or-8?
- predict a molecule's **shape** from electron-pair repulsion (methane
  tetrahedral; water bent), and name lone pairs when they matter?
- explain why **simple molecular substances** are gases, liquids or
  low-melting solids — naming the **intermolecular forces** as what breaks?
- explain the **relative-molecular-mass trend** in melting and boiling
  points across the halogens, and why it holds only for similar series?
- explain why **giant covalent structures** are solids with very high
  melting and boiling points?
- explain **diamond versus graphite versus C₆₀** — hardness, conductivity
  (delocalised electrons!), melting points and solubility — from structure?
- explain why **covalent compounds do not usually conduct electricity**, in
  the two-part marking language?

If any tick wobbles, the section number is in the summary above — go back to
that section, redraw its diagrams, and re-run its quick-check. Bonding is the
foundation Unit 2 electrolysis and the whole of organic chemistry stand on;
make it automatic now and those chapters are free marks.
:::
